title: First impressions of Tokyo, the Ginza and a surprise modern city
summary: Tokyo amazed him with subways, steam trains run by children, stores and a theatre where he played the pipe organ.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: So anyway, we go into Yokohama, they put us off the boat in Yokohama, and take us over into...was it Tokyo...? They take us into Tokyo. And they put us up in a hotel, and we come out the hotel and we looken the town over. It's just like you'd come from out in the country somewhere and the first time you come to New York City, you look like you're in a different world altogether. That's the way Tokyo was to the rest of this trip we had been on.

And we're standing on the corner of what they call the Ginza, that's like Broadway downtown... They had their little... The merchants had their little things out in the sidewalk, selling their goods, and the people are going by, payin' nobody no attention, minding their own business. We were no novelty to them. They would look at you, but they... You know, they just kept right on their business. And they couldn't speak no English, and we could speak very little Japanese. I couldn't speak any. Louis Bacon, he could speak a little Japanese -- very little. But he was the only one in the group who could. I don't know, he's a devil at heart.

But we was standin' out there, and we were noticin' the city of Tokyo... And we were noticin' what they had there. Because when we went there, we... All I had ever heard was that they had grass huts in Japan. And here I'm standing on

the corner, right in front of the subway station, the subway... I never even knew they had a subway. There's a subway, then there's a railroad station, and they had steam trains in the railroad. And a bunch of kids are runnin' the trains. You look up in the cab of the train, you see about eight or ten kids in there, little kids. So they're runnin' the trains with all the men being in the Service, you know. All the men are in the Service, and there's children all over the place -- young people, kids, women. And the place is just racked with humanity.

Then you start looking at the stores. They had stores just like they have here in New York. And there is a big theatre there. So we walked in the theatre. The doors are open. It was closed, but I mean, we could walk in. They had a big organ sittin' in there, a big pipe organ. And I went over and played the organ. "Boy," I said, "ain't that somethin'." I can't do this to the Roxy. I can't just walk into the Roxy and play the organ or the Paramount, but I can come over in Japan; I can walk right in and start playing on the organ.

But it was a beautiful theatre. And truthfully speaking, when I... At that time, I would put Tokyo up with being' the next best city I've ever been in to New York -- even better than Chicago. It looked better. The people
treat you better anyway. But I mean, the city itself. It was as modern, it was more modern than any city in this country outside of New York. And that was in 1946.

You talk about somebody being amazed, it was me! I'm lookin' for grass huts and things. No, there were no grass huts. And the people, when you talk to 'em, they were so sensitive. You know what I mean? They wasn't laughing and grinning in your face, don't know what you were saying. They are very intelligent people.
